Lumminary Opelousas, Louisiana
A History

Opelousas

Founded in 1720. Burned by its own politics in 1868. Built, again and again, by people who were never asked if they wanted the job.

1720

A Trading Post, Not a Town.

The French called it Poste des Opelousas, named for the people who were already here. It was a stop on the trail before it was a city — cattle, hides, French and Spanish colonists, and the people they enslaved to work the prairie.

Opelousas didn't begin as an idea. It began as a transaction.

Every old town likes to say it has deep roots. Few are honest about what was planted with them.

Manon Baldwin Owned the Corner Across From the Courthouse.

She was born enslaved sometime in the 1770s. Freed in 1809 by the Opelousas lawyer whose name she then carried. She built a boarding house, a tavern, a cleaning business that served the same courthouse and jail that had once held people like her. Locals called the intersection Manon's Corner.

A few miles outside town, Martin Donato ran one of the largest estates in the parish. He was a free man of color. He also owned seventy people.

Freedom in Opelousas was never one thing. It was a status, not a guarantee — and it didn't always mean what you'd want it to mean.

History doesn't resolve into heroes and villains. It resolves into people, making choices inside systems they didn't build and couldn't escape.

Before 1865

The Economy Had a Name, and It Wasn't Subtle.

Cotton. Cattle. Sugar, further south. All of it required hands, and the hands were not paid. St. Landry Parish's wealth — the brick storefronts, the courthouse, the plantation houses still standing on the back roads — was financed by people who owned nothing, including themselves.

This isn't a detour from the story. It is the story's foundation.

A place can be beautiful and built on something ugly at the same time. Opelousas is proof you can hold both without flinching.

September 1868

They Voted. Then They Were Killed for It.

After the Civil War, Black men in St. Landry Parish voted for the first time. In the spring of 1868, that vote nearly elected a Republican government. White Democrats noticed.

In September, a white mob beat a Republican newspaper editor for teaching Black children at a Freedmen's school. Black residents who came to his defense were jailed. The next night, a crowd of roughly two thousand armed white residents gathered in town. The twenty-seven men held in the jail were taken out and shot. Over the following two weeks, an estimated two hundred to two hundred fifty Black residents were killed across the parish.

It is remembered as the Opelousas Massacre — among the deadliest single episodes of Reconstruction-era violence in the United States. In the presidential election that November, seven weeks later, not one vote in St. Landry Parish was cast for Ulysses S. Grant.

The message was the point. It worked for almost a century.

Some history doesn't get a redemptive ending on the next page. This is one of those.

They Built the School Anyway.

For most of the next hundred years, Opelousas was segregated by law — schools, churches, courthouses, the sidewalks themselves in practice if not in writing. Holy Ghost Catholic Church, established for Black Catholics who weren't welcome to worship alongside white parishioners, grew into the largest Black Catholic congregation in the country. The Opelousas Colored School opened in 1919, the first public school for Black children in the city, staffed and funded on a fraction of what white schools received.

None of it was offered. All of it was built, brick by brick, by people working around a system designed to keep them small.

Endurance isn't the same as forgiveness. It's just what was left to do.

Zydeco Didn't Start With an Accordion.

It started in the fields, generations earlier — enslaved people keeping rhythm with hands and feet because instruments weren't theirs to have. The tradition was called juré: call and response, handclaps, no melody you'd recognize as music yet, just survival set to time.

By 1900, juré had become la la — house parties, fiddles, accordions traded across the color line between Creole and Cajun families. After the war, Opelousas's own Clifton Chenier fused it with blues and rhythm and blues and gave it a name that stuck: zydeco, from "les haricots sont pas salés" — the snap beans aren't salty, an old way of saying times are hard.

The music didn't erase what came before it. It carried it forward, on purpose, in a key you could dance to.

Joy built from hardship isn't a metaphor here. It's the literal lineage, verse to verse, field to dance hall.

Opelousas was never one story. It was the trading post and the massacre. The free woman who owned a corner downtown and the free man who owned seventy people. The hundred years of Jim Crow and the song that outlasted it.

What do you do with a place that holds all of that at once?
